sword.name: Sword (arming sword)
sword.notes: Baseline weapon; the Visby tables are applied unchanged.

axe.name: Axe (hand or long-hafted)
axe.notes: Visby work describes axes taking the legs out; leg bias reflects that. Heavy cuts bite through mail (ignores 1 step vs cut).

spiked_club.name: Spiked club / morning star (knout)
spiked_club.notes: Square skull perforations at Visby match a spiked club (Randolph-Quinney et al., 2026); head bias reflects that. Spikes punch through mail (ignores 1 step vs pierce).

spear.name: Spear / lance
spear.notes: Thrusting weapon aimed at the centre mass and face over the shield rim.

bow.name: Bow (war arrows)
bow.notes: Its own table is the US Army's 1865-71 arrow-wound reports (Plains and Apache bows, iron and flint heads). At Visby, 126 arrow and crossbow-bolt wounds fell much like the blade wounds, mostly on the lower body, so on the Visby tables it uses their weights unchanged. Arrows are pierce wounds, not gunfire: bleeding, deep tracks and infection; a barbed head left inside causes trouble for months.

crossbow.name: Crossbow (bolts)
crossbow.notes: Visby's arrow and bolt wounds are counted together (126), mostly on the lower body; the Visby weights are used with a small head bias for aimed shots at the face and helmet. Heavy bolts punch through mail (ignores 1 step vs pierce): design estimate.

sling.name: Sling (stones, lead bullets)
sling.notes: No battlefield tally separates sling wounds. Andean skeletons from the Wari era show cranial trauma in about a quarter to a third of adults, much of it consistent with sling stones, but the cause is not counted apart. Head bias is a design estimate. Blunt: fractures and shock; a helmet takes the edge off (crush steps).

dagger.name: Dagger / knife
dagger.notes: Grappling and finishing weapon. On medieval tables it seeks gaps at neck, face and armpit; elsewhere it uses the forensic knife-assault table as recorded.

bayonet.name: Bayonet (musket or rifle)
bayonet.notes: Rolls on the Peninsular War table, which records where 97 bayonet wounds fell (thighs most, then arms and hands, then chest). Rare in every war with records: 3% of French officers' wounds in Spain, and under 1% of Civil War wounds (922 sabre and bayonet wounds together). The zone bias is used only on tables with raw weapon biases.

entrenching_tool.name: Sharpened entrenching tool (spade)
entrenching_tool.notes: Edges sharpened from 1915 for trench raids; used at Stalingrad and taught to Soviet Spetsnaz. Short overhead chops in a confined space: head, neck and collarbone. No wound data exists; shaped on the Visby axe and club evidence.

saber.name: Sabre or broadsword
saber.notes: Rolls on the Peninsular War table, which records where 284 sword wounds fell: a third on the head and face, then arms, hands and shoulders. Cuts from horseback. The zone bias is used only on tables with raw weapon biases.

lance.name: Cavalry lance
lance.notes: Polish and French lancers, British lancers after 1816. Rolls on the Peninsular War table (43 lance wounds: arms and hands, chest, head). Long reach against men on foot or fleeing.

musket_butt.name: Clubbed musket (butt stroke)
musket_butt.notes: Swung like a club when there was no time to reload or no bayonet. Revolutionary War pensioners lost eyes and had skulls broken by it. Rolls on the Visby melee table with no shield; head bias is a design estimate.

punch.name: Punch
punch.notes: Punches land head and body; leg strikes are kicks.

kick.name: Kick
kick.notes: Most landed kicks are low kicks and body kicks.

matchlock_musket.name: Matchlock musket
matchlock_musket.notes: Heavy infantry musket fired from a rest or the shoulder; a lead ball of about .70-.80 calibre. On the Lützen table it uses the 32 recorded gunshot injuries (mostly carbines and pistols; no source separates musket hits).

wheellock_pistol.name: Wheellock pistol or carbine (cavalry)
wheellock_pistol.notes: Cuirassiers and harquebusiers fired pistols and carbines at close range, aimed at the head and the left side of the chest. On the Lützen table it uses the 32 recorded gunshot injuries, 22 of them to the skull.

musket_smoothbore.name: Smoothbore musket (Brown Bess, Charleville)
musket_smoothbore.notes: Soft lead ball of about .69-.75 calibre. On the Peninsular table it uses the 3,331 recorded musket and rifle wounds; elsewhere the table's pooled odds.

rifle_flintlock.name: Flintlock rifle (Pennsylvania, Baker, Jäger)
rifle_flintlock.notes: Riflemen and Jäger picked off officers and gunners at long range. No source records rifle wounds apart from musket wounds; the slight head bias is a design estimate and applies only on tables with raw weapon biases.

pistol_flintlock.name: Flintlock pistol
pistol_flintlock.notes: Cavalry and officers' sidearm; one shot, then the sword.

artillery_smoothbore.name: Smoothbore artillery (round shot, canister, grape, shell)
artillery_smoothbore.notes: Round shot took off limbs; canister and grape acted like giant shotgun loads; shells burst. On the Peninsular table it uses the 209 recorded ordnance wounds, which fell lower on the body than musket wounds (legs and feet). Three times as lethal as musketry there.

rifle_musket.name: Rifle-musket (Minie ball)
rifle_musket.notes: Soft lead .58 ball; shatters rather than drills bone.

artillery_acw.name: Artillery (canister, shell fragments)
artillery_acw.notes: Canister balls and jagged fragments; heavy fragments crush.

rifle_service.name: Service rifle (bolt or semi-auto, 1914-53)
rifle_service.notes: Lee-Enfield, Mauser, Springfield, Garand, Mosin. Aimed fire at whatever shows.

rifle_assault.name: Assault rifle (M16, AK)
rifle_assault.notes: Intermediate cartridge. Common steel-core AK rounds count as rifle, not armour-piercing.

rifle_ap.name: Rifle, armour-piercing ammunition
rifle_ap.notes: Hardened-core rounds that defeat SAPI plates; ESAPI is rated against them.

machine_gun.name: Machine gun
machine_gun.notes: Grazing fire sweeps low across the ground.

pistol_smg.name: Pistol or submachine gun
pistol_smg.notes: Handgun cartridges; soft armour stops them.

hand_grenade.name: Hand grenade
hand_grenade.notes: Bursts on or near the ground: legs and lower body take most fragments.

mortar_artillery.name: Mortar, rocket or artillery
mortar_artillery.notes: Air and ground bursts; fragments come down onto the head, shoulders and back of prone men.

rpg.name: RPG (rocket-propelled grenade)
rpg.notes: Blast plus fragments; often aimed at vehicles and bunkers.

mine_ied.name: Mine, booby trap or IED
mine_ied.notes: Buried and tripwire devices: feet, legs and groin. Crush covers blast and traumatic amputation.

punji_stake.name: Punji stake
punji_stake.notes: Sharpened, often fouled bamboo in pits and trails; 2% of Vietnam wounds. Pierce wounds carry high infection risk.

explosive_fragment.name: Fragments, unspecified (shell, grenade, mine)
explosive_fragment.notes: Used where a source only says 'fragments' or 'explosion'.

visby-1361-evidence.name: Visby 1361 - bone evidence
visby-1361-evidence.label: Bone evidence (skeletons)
visby-1361-evidence.context: Melee, Gotland peasant levy (mail, shields, few helmets) vs Danish professional troops.
visby-1361-evidence.armor_note: These weights are where blows left marks on bone, so the defenders' armour is already baked in (mail and shields kept blades off the torso). When using this table, do not also subtract torso armour - or use the adjusted table instead.
visby-1361-evidence.status: PLACEHOLDER. Weights fitted to published summaries: lower legs (left heaviest) dominate, then skull, then arms; almost no blade marks on ribs. Replace with Ingelmark's per-bone counts when the chapter is available.
sources: Thordeman, B. (ed.), Armour from the Battle of Wisby 1361, vol. I, 1939 - ch. IV, Ingelmark, B. E., 'The Skeletons', p. 149ff. (NOT YET READ - counts pending)
Summary figures: 1,185 individuals; 456 cut wounds; head wounds in 42.3% / 52.3% / 5.4% of graves 1-3 (Ingelmark, via Medievalists.net 2024).
Swedish History Museum: visible wounds concentrate on arms, legs and skulls; torso protected by mail and shields.

visby-1361-adjusted.name: Visby 1361 - gameplay-adjusted
visby-1361-adjusted.label: Gameplay-adjusted (before armour)
visby-1361-adjusted.context: Same fight as the evidence table, re-weighted to where blows land before armour.
visby-1361-adjusted.armor_note: These weights are where blows LAND. Resolve armour separately using the location's armour slot (body.yaml). Use this table when your system tracks armour coverage.
visby-1361-adjusted.status: Corrections applied to the bone evidence: (1) Torso raised to ~27%: blows that mail stopped, and soft-tissue belly and chest wounds, leave no bone marks. (2) Thighs raised: deep muscle wounds often miss the femur. (3) Lower-leg dominance kept but reduced; the shield-side (left) bias kept. (4) Head lowered slightly: some skull wounds are blows struck after a man fell.
sources: Derived from visby-1361-evidence.

lutzen-1632-mass-grave.name: Lützen 1632 - mass grave (bone evidence)
lutzen-1632-mass-grave.label: Bone evidence: mass grave of 47
lutzen-1632-mass-grave.context: Battle injuries on 47 men buried in one grave at Lützen, most likely infantry of the Swedish Blue Brigade cut down by imperial cavalry. Killed only.
lutzen-1632-mass-grave.armor_note: The men wore little or no armour ('insufficient head protection', the authors note), so armour can be applied. This is bone evidence: wounds to soft tissue, above all the belly and chest, left no mark, so the trunk is under-counted. Some blunt facial fractures may come from the burial rather than the battle. For play, use the all-hits table.
lutzen-1632-mass-grave.status: Historical, from one small grave (47 men, 69 reliable injuries) and one moment of the battle: a cavalry charge with pistols and carbines aimed at the head, as contemporary instructions advised. Not a picture of the whole war.
sources: Nicklisch N., Ramsthaler F., Meller H., Friederich S., Alt K.W., 'The face of war: Trauma analysis of a mass grave from the Battle of Lützen (1632)', PLoS ONE 12(5): e0178252 (2017), open access (PMC5439951): Tables 1, 3 and 4.
Same study: lead balls in the grave were mostly from carbines (12-14), then muskets (5) and pistols (1-3); 21 men had gunshot wounds to the head; the attack came mainly from the front and side.
Injury tally: data/sources/lutzen-1632-mass-grave.csv.
lutzen-1632-mass-grave.confidence_note: Counted from the study's tables of reliable battle injuries (69: 32 projectile, 21 blunt, 16 sharp), each weapon rolling on its own mechanism's injuries. Sides are as recorded; injuries the authors only call probable are left out. Where a bone could belong to more than one location (vertebra, ribcage, cranial base), it is shared by body exposure.

thirty-years-war-all-hits.name: Thirty Years' War - all hits (gameplay)
thirty-years-war-all-hits.label: All hits: gameplay blend
thirty-years-war-all-hits.context: Where shot and blows land on a man in the open, before death and burial sort the evidence. For pike-and-shot battles of the 1600s.
thirty-years-war-all-hits.armor_note: Use this table for gunfire in play; armour applies (cuirassier, harquebusier and pikeman kits). Sabres and clubbed muskets roll on their own tables (the Peninsular records and the Visby melee table).

revolution-1775-83-pensioners.name: American Revolution 1775-83 - disabled veterans' wounds
revolution-1775-83-pensioners.label: Wounded: invalid pension lists 1792-95
revolution-1775-83-pensioners.context: Where Continental soldiers, militiamen and seamen were wounded, from the federal invalid pension lists of 1792-95. Men disabled for life who survived.
revolution-1775-83-pensioners.armor_note: Nobody wore armour, so these are hits before armour. But they are survivors with a lasting disability: wounds that killed (most head, chest and belly wounds) are missing, and limb wounds that left a man lame are over-represented. Use the all-hits table for play.
revolution-1775-83-pensioners.status: Historical, from a pension roll rather than a battlefield count. Entries for sickness, ruptures, frostbite, falls, work accidents and accidental discharges were left out. The pattern (head and neck 12%, trunk 23%, arms 36%, legs 29%) is close to the Civil War wounded (11/18/36/35), which suggests the same survivor effect.
sources: Federal Revolutionary War Invalid Pension Claims, 1792-1795 (573 veterans), Magazine of Early American Datasets, University of Pennsylvania, 2021; from the Secretary of War's lists printed in American State Papers, Claims, vol. 1.
Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/revolution-invalid-pensions-1792-95.csv. The weapon mix counts the 251 wounds whose cause is stated.
revolution-1775-83-pensioners.confidence_note: Counted wound by wound from 344 men's entries (379 wounds whose site is named; 32 more not located). Sides are recorded for about half and were close to even (85 left, 99 right), so left and right are pooled and split by body exposure (design estimate). 'Arm' without more detail is shared between upper arm and forearm.

peninsular-1808-14-officers.name: Peninsular War 1808-14 - French officers' wounds
peninsular-1808-14-officers.label: Wounded and killed: French officers' records
peninsular-1808-14-officers.context: Where French officers were hit in Spain and Portugal, 1808-1814, by musket, sabre, bayonet, lance and cannon. Mostly men who survived.
peninsular-1808-14-officers.armor_note: Almost no one wore body armour (cuirassiers and carabiniers had steel cuirasses, and dragoons and heavy cavalry helmets), so armour can be applied. The records are of men who survived far more often than of men killed (146 killed and 84 died of wounds against 4,129 wounded), so head and trunk hits from gunfire are under-counted: use the all-hits table for gunfire in play. Edged weapons rarely killed (8 deaths among 424 sword, bayonet and lance casualties), so their columns are close to every hit they made.
peninsular-1808-14-officers.status: Historical. French officers, so mounted officers and men in the front rank are over-represented; the rank-and-file sample was hit in the head more often (24%). Tables 7 and 8 were read from the article's table images.
sources: Planas Campos J. and Grajal de Blas A., 'Wounds & Weapons in the Napoleonic War: a database of the Peninsular War', British Journal for Military History 7(3), Nov 2021, pp. 117-127: Table 1 (weapons, 4,359 entries), Table 2 (locations, 3,995 events), Tables 6-8 (location by firearm, edged weapon and ordnance). Source registers: French Army officer files, SHD 2Yb.
Same article, Table 11: 491 rank and file of the 100e de ligne - arms 22%, legs 40%, chest 6%, head 24%, abdomen 1%, shoulder 7% (officers: 26/44/4/14/3/9).
Comparison quoted there: Austrian officers wounded at Austerlitz (Guiga 2021) - upper limbs 26%, lower limbs 45%, head 6%, upper body 9%, back 4%.
peninsular-1808-14-officers.confidence_note: Location counts are from the source (3,995 wound events). Each weapon rolls on its own recorded distribution (musket 2,848, sword 284, bayonet 97, lance 43, ordnance 209 wounds). Left and right are not recorded and are split evenly; 'arm' (bras) is put on the upper arm because wrist and forearm are listed apart. Rifles and pistols use the musket data.

peninsular-1808-14-all-hits.name: Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay)
peninsular-1808-14-all-hits.label: All hits: gameplay blend
peninsular-1808-14-all-hits.context: Where musket balls and shot land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records. Use for the Peninsula, Waterloo and the War of 1812.

peninsular-1808-14-all-hits.status: Estimated. The Peninsular records hold only 146 killed outright (head and chest most often), too few to use, so the Civil War killed-in-action table (also soft lead balls) stands in for the dead. Edit the share in tools/blend_tables.py if you prefer another.

indian-wars-1865-71-arrows.name: Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons)
indian-wars-1865-71-arrows.label: Arrow hits: Army surgeons' reports
indian-wars-1865-71-arrows.context: Soldiers, scouts and civilians hit by arrows on the Plains and in the Southwest, mostly 1866-70. Killed and wounded together.
indian-wars-1865-71-arrows.armor_note: The men hit wore no armour, so these are hits before armour: armour can be applied. A mounted man's legs are partly covered by the horse, and many of these men were cavalry; that is one reason leg hits are rare here (9%) while Visby's arrow wounds were mostly in the legs.
indian-wars-1865-71-arrows.status: Historical, but a collection of case reports, not a census: striking trunk and skull cases were more likely to be written up. The 40 cases taken from routine casualty lists (none fatal) are less biased and still show 40% of wounds in the trunk. Several of the men had been hit by 3 to 9 arrows each.
sources: US Surgeon General's Office, Circular No. 3: A Report of Surgical Cases Treated in the Army of the United States from 1865 to 1871 (Washington, 1871), 'Arrow-Wounds', pp. 144-161, cases 451-487. Full text: archive.org item reportofsurgical00unituoft.
Same report, p. 161: of 83 cases, 26 'proved fatal', including nearly all that entered the skull, chest or abdomen; 7 of 9 penetrating abdominal wounds were fatal.
Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/indian-wars-arrows-1865-71.csv.

wwii-italy-1944-killed.name: WWII Italy 1944 - killed in action
wwii-italy-1944-killed.label: Italy 1944: killed in action
wwii-italy-1944-killed.context: Wounds on 983 American soldiers killed by missiles (bullets and shell fragments), examined in Italian military cemeteries, 1944. 7,006 wounds.

severity.name: Light
severity.guide: Damage well under what your system treats as a serious hit (e.g. < 1/3 of a wound level / HP threshold).

severity.name: Serious
severity.guide: A solid hit: about 1/3 to 2/3 of a threshold, or a hit that beat armour by a clear margin.

severity.name: Critical
severity.guide: A crippling or killing blow: over 2/3 of a threshold, or a critical success.

ballistic.note: Used for every hit from a firearm or explosive (any weapon with a threat level), including a blast's crush wounds. Calibrated to Bougainville 1944, where 38-42% of head, chest and abdomen hits killed but only 0.3% of arm and 3.4% of leg hits did. If your own system sets severity, give gunshots to the head and trunk its harshest damage.

cut.name: Cut
cut.desc: Edge blow: opens soft tissue; can sever limbs.

pierce.name: Pierce
pierce.desc: Point or spike: small entry, deep track; internal damage and infection.

crush.name: Crush
crush.desc: Blunt impact: fractures and shock; less external bleeding.

ballistic.name: Ballistic
ballistic.desc: Bullet, ball or shell fragment: shatters bone, carries cloth and dirt deep into the wound.

bleed.1: Slow - seeping; lose 1 Blood per minute
bleed.2: Heavy - lose 1 Blood per round; bind within minutes
bleed.3: Arterial - lose 3 Blood per round; tourniquet or pressure now

lethal.days: Fatal in days without care (infection, internal damage)

impair.dazed: Stunned: lose next action, then -20% for 1d6 rounds
impair.unconscious: Knocked out (check each minute to wake)
impair.vision: Vision impaired: -30% to sight-based actions; blinded if both eyes
impair.breath: Winded: no sustained exertion; fatigue doubled
impair.collapse: Collapses; can only crawl or crouch
impair.grip: Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it
impair.leg: Movement halved; -20% to footwork and dodging

flags.shock: Shock check: endurance roll or be stunned 1d6 rounds
flags.fracture: Bone broken: no use of the part until set; pain +1 when used
flags.severed: Part severed: arterial bleeding until cauterised or tourniqueted

thresholds.effect: Pale and weak: -10% to all actions
Faint check each minute; -20% to all actions
Barely conscious: -40% to all actions, can only crawl

tourniquet.note: Limb only: stops bleeding; limb lost if left on for hours

modifiers.name: Target fleeing (back turned)
modifiers.desc: Rout: back, back of the head and legs exposed; front almost unreachable.

modifiers.name: Target flanked (two or more attackers)
modifiers.desc: Visby team-fighting: one engages the front while others strike from behind and low.
modifiers.notes: From the Visby reading of attackers working in teams (Randolph-Quinney et al., 2026).

modifiers.name: Target has no shield
modifiers.desc: Tables assume a shield. Without one the body and head are more open.

modifiers.name: Target warding with arms (unarmed or disarmed)
modifiers.desc: Defensive wounds: forearms and hands raised to block.
modifiers.notes: Defensive forearm and hand wounds are recorded at Towton and in modern sharp-force forensics.

modifiers.name: Target behind cover (breastwork, wall, trench)
modifiers.desc: Only head, shoulders and arms show over the parapet.
modifiers.notes: For entrenched or firing-line fighting. Gunfire tables only by default.

called_shot.rule: Roll location twice; keep the roll in the called zone. If both or neither land there, keep the first.

cavalry_helmet.name: Cavalry helmet (brass or steel, with crest)

flak_steel.name: Steel plates in fabric (aircrew flak vest)

kits.name: Rawhide shield, no armour (Plains warrior)
kits.notes: Round shield of thick, shrunken buffalo hide. It could turn arrows and glancing balls, but covered nothing by itself: use the shield situations.

kits.name: Gotland levy: mail coif, padded coat
kits.notes: Many Visby dead were buried wearing mail coifs.

kits.name: Gotland, better equipped: coif, coat of plates
kits.notes: Coats of plates and plate gauntlets were recovered from the Visby graves.

kits.name: Danish man-at-arms (1361)
kits.notes: Professional kit of the period; face left open (visors uncertain for 1361).

kits.name: Cuirassier, three-quarter armour (1630s)
kits.notes: Closed helmet, proofed breastplate, arm defences and tassets to the knee; one gauntlet (the bridle hand). Heavy, and going out of use by the 1640s.

kits.name: Harquebusier: buff coat, breastplate, pot helmet
kits.notes: Lighter cavalry of the Thirty Years' War and the English Civil War: 'lobster-tail' pot helmet, breast and back plate over a buff coat, a gauntlet on the bridle arm.

kits.name: Pikeman: morion and corslet
kits.notes: Open helmet, breast and back plates and short tassets. Many pikemen left the armour behind on campaign.

kits.name: Cuirassier: steel cuirass and helmet
kits.notes: French cuirassiers and carabiniers; breast and back plates were proofed against musket balls at range (1 step), better against pistols. The skirt of the cuirass left the belly partly open.

kits.name: Dragoon or light dragoon helmet
kits.notes: Brass, steel or leather helmet with a crest, worn by dragoons on both sides; turned sabre cuts.

kits.name: Private steel vest (Civil War, 1862)
kits.notes: Atwater and G&D Cook vests, sold by the thousand in 1862; about 8 lb, most were thrown away on the march.

kits.name: Steel helmet and Sappenpanzer (WWI German sentry)
kits.notes: Heavy plate issued to sentries and machine gunners in static positions; too heavy for the attack.

kits.name: Aircrew flak vest and helmet (WWII bomber crew)
kits.notes: Steel plates sewn into fabric against flak fragments; worn by US bomber crews from 1943.

kits.name: Steel helmet only (1915-1950s rifleman)
kits.notes: Most infantry from 1915 to the early 1950s wore a steel helmet and no body armour.

kits.name: M1 helmet, nylon flak vest (US Army M1952/M69, 1952-75)
kits.notes: M69 nylon vest stopped fragments and low-velocity pistol rounds, not an AK-47 round.

kits.name: M1 helmet, Doron vest (USMC M1951/M1955, 1951-75)
kits.notes: Doron fibreglass plates over the chest, sides and back; nylon over the upper torso. Stopped .45 ACP at the muzzle, not rifle rounds.

kits.name: PASGT vest and helmet (1980s-90s)
kits.notes: Kevlar against fragments and handgun rounds; no rifle plates.

kits.name: Ranger Body Armor, front plate only (Mogadishu 1993)
kits.notes: IIIA soft vest with a single ceramic plate in front; the first version had no back plate, so only about half the usual plate coverage.

kits.name: Interceptor vest, SAPI plates, ACH (2000s)
kits.notes: Plates cover the centre of the chest and back (about 65% of upper-torso hits); soft Kevlar elsewhere on the vest. Neck, groin and shoulder pieces were not always worn.

kits.name: Plate carrier, ESAPI plates, helmet (2010s-)
kits.notes: Lighter than a full vest: plates over the vital area, soft side panels only. Outside the plates is a gap.

kits.name: Concealable soft vest (police IIIA)
kits.notes: Stops handgun rounds, not rifles. Soft Kevlar gives little protection against a knife (pierce 0).

sources: Visby kit contents follow the finds summarised in Thordeman (1939): mail coifs, coats of plates, gauntlets. Not yet checked against the text.
Vietnam vests: M1952/M69 nylon stopped fragments and low-velocity pistol rounds but not rifle rounds; M1955 Doron plates stopped .45 ACP at the muzzle (Wikipedia, 'Flak jacket').
Protection steps and coverage percentages are design estimates.

Visby 1361.summary: King Valdemar IV Atterdag of Denmark invaded Gotland, then a rich trading island, and met its rural defenders outside the walls of Visby. The Gotlanders were a peasant levy facing professional troops, and the fight became a slaughter. The dead were buried quickly in mass graves, many still in their armour, which is why Visby gives the best picture of medieval battle wounds: 1,185 skeletons were recovered from three graves.

sides.name: Danish army
sides.who: Professional soldiers of Valdemar IV.
sides.armour: Mail, coats of plates and plate helmets; the best-equipped wore gauntlets and leg harness. Few of their dead are in the graves.

sides.name: Gotlandic levy
sides.who: Farmers and freeholders of rural Gotland, called out to defend the island.
sides.armour: Uneven. Many wore mail coifs and padded coats; some had coats of plates and gauntlets; many had little or nothing on the legs, which took most of the blade wounds.

examples.name: Gotland levy
examples.notes: Coif and padded coat; legs bare.

examples.name: Gotland freeholder
examples.notes: Wealthier farmer in a coat of plates.

examples.name: Danish sergeant
examples.notes: Coat of plates and mail; the spiked club matches square holes in Visby skulls.

examples.name: Danish crossbowman
examples.notes: 126 arrow and bolt wounds were found among the Gotland dead.

sources: Swedish History Museum, 'Skull from the Battle of Visby'.
Medievalists.net, 'Medieval battle injuries' (2024), summarising Ingelmark in Thordeman (1939).

Thirty Years' War.summary: A war of religion and power across the Holy Roman Empire: the Catholic Emperor and the Catholic League against Protestant princes, joined by Denmark, then Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus, and finally France. It was the age of pike and shot: squares of pikemen with musketeers on their flanks, and cavalry that fought with pistols and carbines as much as swords. At Lützen, near Leipzig, on 16 November 1632 the Swedes beat Wallenstein's imperial army but Gustavus Adolphus was killed. A mass grave of 47 men found there in 2011 is most likely part of the Swedish 'Blue Brigade', surprised in the flank by imperial cavalry; it is the source of this group's table.

sides.name: Sweden and Protestant allies
sides.who: Swedish and Finnish troops and many German and Scottish mercenaries in Swedish pay, with Saxony and other Protestant states.
sides.armour: Pikemen wore helmets and corslets when they kept them; musketeers wore none; cavalry rode in buff coats with helmets and breastplates.

sides.name: Imperial army and Catholic League
sides.who: The Emperor's army under Wallenstein and Pappenheim, Bavaria and the Catholic League, and Croat light horse.
sides.armour: Cuirassiers in three-quarter plate, harquebusiers in buff coat and breastplate, pikemen in corslets; Croats and musketeers unarmoured.

examples.name: Blue Brigade musketeer
examples.notes: Matchlock and bandolier; clubs the musket in the press.

examples.name: Finnish hakkapeliitta
examples.notes: Light cavalry: pistols, then swords at the gallop.

examples.name: Imperial cuirassier
examples.notes: Pappenheim's heavy horse; pistols at close range, aimed at the head.

examples.name: Imperial harquebusier
examples.notes: Carbine and pistols; most of the balls in the Lützen grave are carbine shot.

sources: Nicklisch et al., PLoS ONE 12(5): e0178252 (2017): the Lützen mass grave, the Blue Brigade, and contemporary advice to aim for the head and left chest.
Sides, armour and dress: general historical knowledge, not from the grave study.

American Revolution.summary: The thirteen colonies, joined by France from 1778 and later Spain and the Dutch Republic, fought Britain for independence. Battles were fought with smoothbore muskets and bayonets at close range, with artillery firing round shot, grape and canister; riflemen picked off officers from cover; dragoons fought with the sabre. Bayonet charges decided many fights, and some ended in killings of men trying to surrender, such as Paoli (1777) and Waxhaws (1780). Peckham counted 7,174 Americans killed and 8,241 wounded in action. The tables here are tallied from the men disabled for life who claimed federal invalid pensions in 1792-95.

sides.name: Continental Army and militia
sides.who: Continental regulars, state militia, riflemen, light dragoons, and the Continental Navy and privateers.
sides.armour: None. Officers wore a small gorget as a mark of rank; light dragoons wore leather helmets.

sides.name: British Army and Loyalists
sides.who: British regulars and marines, Loyalist provincial regiments and rangers, and the Royal Navy.
sides.armour: None. Grenadiers' bearskin caps and light infantry caps gave no protection; light dragoons wore crested leather helmets.

sides.name: German auxiliaries
sides.who: Regiments hired from Hesse-Kassel, Brunswick and other German states ('Hessians'), including Jäger riflemen.
sides.armour: None; grenadiers wore brass-fronted mitre caps, which were not armour.

sides.name: French forces
sides.who: Rochambeau's expeditionary army and the French navy, from 1778; decisive at Yorktown in 1781.
sides.armour: None.

sides.name: Native nations
sides.who: Warriors on both sides: most of the Mohawk, Seneca and Cherokee fought with Britain; the Oneida and Tuscarora with the Americans.
sides.armour: None. Musket, tomahawk and knife; raids and ambushes on the frontier.

examples.name: Morgan's rifleman
examples.notes: Long rifle, slow to load, deadly at range; no bayonet.

examples.name: British grenadier
examples.notes: The bayonet charge was the British infantry's favoured tactic.

examples.name: British light dragoon
examples.notes: Tarleton's British Legion fought with sabres at Waxhaws.

examples.name: Hessian Jäger
examples.notes: German hunters' rifle, short and accurate.

sources: Peckham, The Toll of Independence (1974), via Journal of the American Revolution, 'The 25 Deadliest Battles of the Revolutionary War' (2014): 7,174 killed and 8,241 wounded.
Federal Revolutionary War Invalid Pension Claims, 1792-1795, Magazine of Early American Datasets (Penn, 2021).
Sides, alliances and dress: general historical knowledge, not from the pension data.

Napoleonic era & War of 1812.summary: France under Napoleon against shifting coalitions of Britain, Austria, Prussia, Russia, Spain and Portugal. In the Peninsular War (1808-1814) a British and Portuguese army under Wellington, with Spanish armies and guerrillas, drove the French out of Spain; the wound tables come from French officers' files of that war. At the same time (1812-1815) the United States fought Britain in North America, with the same weapons: smoothbore muskets and bayonets, rifles, sabres and smoothbore artillery. Many British regulars in the later War of 1812 were Peninsular veterans. No region-by-region wound count survives for the War of 1812, so it uses these tables.

sides.name: French Empire and allies
sides.who: French line and light infantry, cavalry and artillery, with Polish, German and Italian allies.
sides.armour: Cuirassiers and carabiniers wore steel breastplates and backplates and helmets; dragoons wore brass helmets; infantry wore none.

sides.name: Britain and Peninsular allies
sides.who: Wellington's British and Portuguese army (including the 95th Rifles), Spanish regular armies and guerrillas.
sides.armour: None for infantry; heavy and light dragoons wore helmets. British Household Cavalry wore cuirasses only after 1815.

sides.name: United States (1812-15)
sides.who: US regulars, state militia (including Kentucky riflemen), US Navy and Marines.
sides.armour: None; some light dragoons wore leather helmets.

sides.name: British North America (1812-15)
sides.who: British regulars, Canadian fencibles and militia, the Royal Navy, and the Provincial Marine.
sides.armour: None.

sides.name: Tecumseh's confederacy
sides.who: Shawnee, Potawatomi, Kickapoo and other nations under Tecumseh, allied with Britain until his death at the Thames (1813).
sides.armour: None. Musket, rifle, tomahawk and war club.

examples.name: French cuirassier
examples.notes: Heavy cavalry: straight sword, breastplate and helmet.

examples.name: Polish lancer
examples.notes: Vistula Legion lancers, feared at Albuera (1811).

examples.name: British redcoat
examples.notes: Brown Bess and bayonet, firing in two-deep line.

examples.name: US regular, 1814
examples.notes: Chippawa and Lundy's Lane; Springfield musket.

examples.name: Kentucky militia rifleman
examples.notes: River Raisin, the Thames, New Orleans.

sources: Planas Campos and Grajal de Blas, British Journal for Military History 7(3), 2021 (Peninsular War wound database).
Sides, armour and dress: general historical knowledge, not from the wound data.

American Civil War.summary: The United States (Union) against the seceded Confederate States. Most wounds came from the rifle-musket firing soft lead conoidal balls, which shattered bone and led to the war's many amputations. Artillery, especially canister at close range, did the rest; sabre and bayonet wounds were rare.

sides.name: Union
sides.who: US Regular Army and state volunteer regiments.
sides.armour: None issued. In 1862 private 'bullet-proof vests' (Atwater, G&D Cook) sold by the thousand; at about 8 lb most were thrown away on the march, and wearing one was thought unmanly.

sides.name: Confederacy
sides.who: Confederate States Army and state troops.
sides.armour: None issued; private vests were rarer still.

examples.name: Union volunteer with steel vest, 1862
examples.notes: One of the few who kept his vest.

examples.name: Confederate infantryman
examples.notes: Enfield or Springfield rifle-musket, no armour.

examples.name: Union cavalryman
examples.notes: Sabre charge; carbine and revolver as well.

sources: Antietam on the Web, 'Saved by his steel vest' (2018): Atwater and G&D Cook vests, sales and use.

American Indian Wars.summary: After the Civil War the US Army garrisoned the Plains and the Southwest and fought a long series of campaigns against the nations whose land the railways and settlers were entering: on the Plains the Lakota (Sioux), Cheyenne, Arapaho, Kiowa and Comanche; in Arizona, New Mexico and Texas the Apache, Navajo and Lipan. Most fights were raids, ambushes of herders, mail escorts and wagon trains, and skirmishes between small parties. Warriors used firearms when they could get them; younger and poorer men still fought with the bow, which in skilled hands loosed several arrows in the time a soldier reloaded. The Army's surgeons wrote up 83 arrow cases from 1865-71; the table here is tallied from them.

sides.name: US Army
sides.who: Regular cavalry and infantry posted to frontier forts, with Indian scouts and civilian herders, teamsters and settlers.
sides.armour: None. Wool uniform; the cavalry fought mounted or dismounted with carbine, revolver and sabre.

sides.name: Plains and Southwest nations
sides.who: Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Kiowa, Comanche, Apache, Navajo and Lipan warriors, in raiding and war parties.
sides.armour: None worn. Many warriors carried a round shield of thick rawhide (buffalo hide on the Plains), which could turn an arrow or a glancing ball.

examples.name: Plains warrior with bow
examples.notes: Iron trade-hoop or flint arrowheads; several arrows in quick succession.

examples.name: US cavalry trooper
examples.notes: No arrow-era gunshot table exists; his revolver rolls on a Civil War table.

examples.name: US infantryman
examples.notes: Springfield rifle (rolls on a Civil War table).

examples.name: Indian scout
examples.notes: Several scouts in the reports were themselves hit by arrows.

sources: US Surgeon General's Office, Circular No. 3 (1871), 'Arrow-Wounds', pp. 144-161 (archive.org: reportofsurgical00unituoft). Places, tribes, units and the note on firearms and bows are from the case reports and Dr. Muller's note there.
Rawhide shields: general ethnographic description, not from the report.

WWI.summary: The Allied powers (France, the British Empire, Russia, Italy, and from 1917 the United States) against the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria). Trench warfare made artillery the main killer and the head the most exposed target, which drove the return of the steel helmet.

sides.name: Allies
sides.who: French, British Empire, Russian, Italian and American armies.
sides.armour: Cloth caps and kepis in 1914. Steel helmets from 1915-16: the French Adrian, then the British Brodie. A little private-purchase body armour; Italian assault engineers used heavy plate.

sides.name: Central Powers
sides.who: German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Bulgarian armies.
sides.armour: German Stahlhelm from 1916. Heavy Sappenpanzer breastplates for sentries and machine gunners in fixed positions.

examples.name: German machine gunner
examples.notes: Stahlhelm and Sappenpanzer in a fixed position.

examples.name: Trench raider, 1917
examples.notes: Night raid: sharpened spade, revolver and grenades; no rifle in the trench.

examples.name: Russian infantryman, 1915
examples.notes: Most Russian soldiers had no steel helmet; the army set great store by the bayonet.

examples.name: Italian Ardito, 1918
examples.notes: Assault trooper: Adrian helmet, grenades and dagger.

examples.name: German stormtrooper, 1918
examples.notes: Stahlhelm; grenades, carbine and sharpened spade.

examples.name: Ottoman infantryman, Gallipoli
examples.notes: Cloth headgear, no steel helmet; Mauser rifle.

examples.name: Bulgarian infantryman
examples.notes: Mostly without steel helmets; Mannlicher rifle.

sources: Military Wiki, 'Stahlhelm' (introduction of German and Allied steel helmets).

WWII.summary: The Allies against the Axis. This group's tables come from two theatres: the jungle campaign on Bougainville in the Solomon Islands (US Marines and Army against the Imperial Japanese Army) and the Italian campaign (US, British and Commonwealth forces against the German army). Mortars and artillery caused half of the Bougainville wounds.

sides.name: Allies
sides.who: US Army and Marine Corps; British and Commonwealth armies in Italy; the Australian army, which took over Bougainville from late 1944.
sides.armour: Steel helmets (M1, Brodie) for all infantry, no body armour. Bomber crews wore steel-plate flak vests from 1943.

sides.name: Axis
sides.who: Imperial Japanese Army; German Wehrmacht.
sides.armour: Steel helmets (Japanese Type 90, German Stahlhelm); no infantry body armour.

examples.name: Japanese infantryman
examples.notes: Type 90 helmet; grenades and knee mortars at close range.

examples.name: US bomber waist gunner
examples.notes: Flak vest and helmet; not an infantry kit.

examples.name: Australian infantryman, Bougainville 1945
examples.notes: Often a slouch hat rather than a helmet in the jungle; Owen submachine gun.

examples.name: German paratrooper, Cassino
examples.notes: Rimless paratrooper helmet, MP 40; fought as infantry.

sources: Borden Institute, Weapons Effects and War Wounds, Table 1-1 (Bougainville causes of injury).

Korea.summary: The United Nations Command, led by the United States with South Korea, the British Commonwealth and others, against North Korea and, from late 1950, the Chinese People's Volunteer Army. Fighting swung from mobile war to static trench lines, where body armour first came into general use.

sides.name: UN Command
sides.who: US, South Korean, British Commonwealth and other UN forces.
sides.armour: Steel helmets. The US Marines fielded the M1951 vest with Doron plates; the Army's nylon M-1952 reached front-line troops in late 1952, in small numbers.

sides.name: North Korea and China
sides.who: Korean People's Army; Chinese People's Volunteer Army.
sides.armour: No body armour; many Chinese soldiers had no steel helmet.

examples.name: South Korean infantryman
examples.notes: ROK Army: M1 helmet, M1 Garand.

examples.name: North Korean infantryman, 1950
examples.notes: Korean People's Army: Soviet-pattern kit, often no steel helmet; Mosin rifle or PPSh.

examples.name: Chinese infantryman
examples.notes: Quilted uniform, PPSh submachine gun, grenades.

sources: Wikipedia, 'M-1952 Flak Jacket'.

Vietnam.summary: South Vietnam, the United States and allies (Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, Thailand) against North Vietnam's army (PAVN) and the southern Viet Cong. Most wounds came from fragments; mines and booby traps caused 15% of wounds and punji stakes 2%, while bullets killed far more often than they wounded.

sides.name: US and allies
sides.who: South Vietnamese army (ARVN), US Army and Marine Corps, and Australian, New Zealand, South Korean and Thai contingents.
sides.armour: M1 steel helmet; Army M69 nylon vest, Marine M1955 vest with Doron plates. Both stopped fragments, not AK rounds, and in the heat they were often left behind on patrol.

sides.name: PAVN and Viet Cong
sides.who: People's Army of Vietnam regulars; Viet Cong guerrillas.
sides.armour: None. The PAVN pith helmet gave no ballistic protection. They relied on concealment, mines and booby traps.

examples.name: ARVN infantryman
examples.notes: South Vietnamese army: M1 helmet, usually no vest; M16 from 1968, carbines before.

examples.name: Australian infantryman, 1968
examples.notes: Bush hat, no body armour; L1A1 SLR.

examples.name: Viet Cong guerrilla
examples.notes: Booby traps, mines and punji pits.

sources: Neel, Medical Support of the U.S. Army in Vietnam (1973), ch. 3, Table 6.
Wikipedia, 'Flak jacket' (M69 and M1955 protection).

Late 20th century.summary: Six smaller wars with very different fighting. Northern Ireland (1969-98): the British Army and police against the Provisional IRA, mostly sniping and bombs. The Falklands (1982): Britain against Argentina, infantry fighting over open hills. The Gulf War (1991): a US-led coalition against Iraq. Somalia (1993): US Rangers and special forces against Somali militia in Mogadishu. Chechnya (1994-96 and later): Russia against Chechen separatists, with urban battles in Grozny.

sides.name: Northern Ireland
sides.who: British Army and RUC; Provisional IRA and other paramilitaries.
sides.armour: British patrols wore helmets and soft body armour; the IRA wore none and used rifles, snipers and bombs.

sides.name: Falklands 1982
sides.who: British paratroopers, Royal Marines and infantry; Argentine conscripts and marines.
sides.armour: Steel helmets on both sides; little body armour.

sides.name: Gulf War 1991
sides.who: US-led coalition; Iraqi army.
sides.armour: US troops in PASGT Kevlar helmets and vests (fragments and pistol rounds); Iraqi troops in steel helmets.

sides.name: Somalia 1993
sides.who: US Task Force Ranger; Somali National Alliance militia.
sides.armour: Rangers wore IIIA soft vests with a single ceramic front plate and no back plate; militia were unarmoured, with AKs and RPGs.

sides.name: Chechnya
sides.who: Russian army and interior troops; Chechen separatist fighters.
sides.armour: Russian helmets and body armour, unevenly issued; Chechen fighters largely unarmoured.

examples.name: British soldier, Belfast
examples.notes: Soft body armour and helmet (PASGT used as the nearest kit).

examples.name: British Guardsman, Tumbledown
examples.notes: Steel helmet; the final assaults on the mountains ended with the bayonet.

examples.name: British soldier, Desert Storm
examples.notes: Soft body armour and helmet (PASGT used as the nearest kit).

examples.name: Russian conscript, Grozny 1995
examples.notes: Steel helmet; body armour often missing.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Ranger Body Armor' (front plate only in 1993).
Borden Institute, Weapons Effects and War Wounds, Table 1-2 (wound distributions).

Iraq & Afghanistan.summary: US-led coalitions in Afghanistan from 2001 (against the Taliban and al-Qaeda) and in Iraq from 2003 (against the Iraqi army, then insurgents and militias). Roadside bombs became the main weapon against coalition troops, and modern body armour moved wounds from the torso to the head, face and limbs.

sides.name: Coalition
sides.who: US, British and other allied forces; the Afghan and new Iraqi security forces they trained.
sides.armour: Interceptor vests with SAPI rifle plates and Kevlar helmets from the start of the Iraq war; ESAPI plates against armour-piercing rounds by the mid-2000s; lighter plate carriers later, especially in Afghanistan.

sides.name: Iraqi army, 2003
sides.who: Iraqi regular army and Republican Guard during the invasion.
sides.armour: Steel helmets for some; little body armour.

sides.name: Insurgents and Taliban
sides.who: Iraqi insurgents and militias; Taliban fighters.
sides.armour: Largely unarmoured. IEDs, RPGs, rifles and mortars.

examples.name: British soldier, Helmand 2009
examples.notes: Osprey vest with plates (Interceptor used as the nearest kit).

examples.name: Afghan National Army soldier
examples.notes: Helmet and vest when issued (PASGT used as the nearest kit).

sources: Owens et al., J Trauma 2008; Borden Institute, Table 1-1 (DoD Trauma Registry 2007-17).

Reference.summary: Not a war. The random-hit table shows where hits would land if every square inch of the body were equally likely: use it as a neutral table with any armour, or to see how far a real war's pattern moves away from chance. Below it, the four-war comparison shows how American wound patterns changed from WWII to Iraq and Afghanistan, counted the same way each time; each of those four tables is listed under its own war as the Owens comparison set.

comparison.title: US wars compared: where hospitalized wounded were hit
comparison.note: Same source and counting rule for every row: hospitalized casualties, including men who later died of wounds. With modern body armour the thorax share fell to 6% and the head and neck rose to 30%, because plates cover the chest and nothing covers the face and neck. Gunshot vs explosion shows how the weapon mix shifted.
comparison.source: Owens et al., 'Combat wounds in Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom', J Trauma 2008 (National Academies 2014, Tables 3-2 and 3-4).

Close combat.summary: Knife killings recorded by forensic pathologists: usually one attacker against an unarmoured, often surprised victim, with several wounds each. The table stands in for knives and bayonets on every non-medieval table.

sides.name: Attacker
sides.who: Single assailant with a knife.
sides.armour: None.

sides.name: Victim
sides.who: Usually unarmoured civilians; 41% had defensive wounds on the hands and arms.
sides.armour: None. Soft ballistic vests give little protection against a stab; plates stop one.

examples.name: Police officer
examples.notes: IIIA vest: stops bullets, not knives.

examples.name: Soldier in plates
examples.notes: Plates stop most stabs to the chest.

sources: Karlsson 1998, via forensicmed.co.uk.

Unarmed.summary: Professional mixed martial arts under the Unified Rules: four-ounce gloves, no strikes to the groin, spine or back of the head. The table also stands in for punches, kicks, elbows and knees on every other table.

sides.name: Fighters
sides.who: Professional MMA fighters.
sides.armour: Gloves, mouthguard and groin cup only.

examples.name: Kickboxer
examples.notes: Low kicks to the lead leg.

sources: Fightshow, UFC Strike Map.
